title: SC rules activist’s arrest during ‘GotaGoHome’ protests violated Fundamental Rights - Breaking News | Daily Mirror
summary:
Colombo, July 23 (Daily Mirror) - The Supreme Court today held that the arrest of social activist Anuruddha Bandara during the 2022 “GotaGoHome” protest movement was arbitrary and unlawful, ruling that the police violated his fundamental rights by arresting him without objectively reasonable grounds.

In a judgment delivered today, a three-judge bench comprising Justices Janak De Silva, Dr. Sobhitha Rajakaruna and Menaka Wijesundera found that the petitioner’s rights under Articles 12(1) and 13(1) of the Constitution had been infringed by the then Senior Deputy Inspector General of Police Deshabandu Tennakoon and the Officer-in-Charge of the Colombo North Crimes Investigation Division.

Justice Dr. Sobhitha Rajakaruna delivered the judgment, with the other two judges concurring.

The petitioner had challenged his arrest and detention, alleging that police targeted him because of his criticism of the then government and his support for peaceful anti-government protests during the country’s economic crisis. He maintained that he had used social media to encourage peaceful demonstrations and had consistently urged protesters to remain non-violent.

Saliya Peiris, PC, with Thanuka Nandasiri and Manujaya De Silva appeared for the petitioner while State Counsel Sajith Bandara appeared for the Attorney General.

title: Houthis claim attack on oil tankers as US launches more strikes on Iran - Breaking News | Daily Mirror
summary:
BBC - Yemen's Houthis say they have attacked two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea as the US launched its 12th consecutive night of strikes on Iran.

Iranian state media said two people had been killed in the US strikes on Wednesday, and a tanker caught fire in an explosion in a mined route in the Strait of Hormuz.

Ahead of the latest round of strikes, US President Donald Trump had threatened to destroy an Iranian bridge or power plant if Iran attacked a ship in the strait and to "take care of" the Houthis if they blocked the Red Sea.

If confirmed, the Houthi attack would be the first since the Iran-backed group announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia.

The Houthis named the tankers as the Encelia and the Layla, though their responsibility has not been confirmed.

The group's military spokesperson Yahya Saree said they had targeted the ships with drones and missiles for allegedly violating its naval blockade.

Saree added that the Houthis promised to continue their naval operations and would continue "enforcing the 'siege for a siege' equation".

The state-run Saudi Press Agency confirmed early on Thursday that the Encelia was struck "while sailing in the Red Sea", resulting in a fire on its bow.

Citing an unnamed official source at the Transport General Authority, it described the attack as a violation of international law. All crew were safe, it reported.

UK Maritime Trade Operation (UKMTO) reported an "unknown projectile" struck a Saudi tanker about 130km from Al Shuqaiq in Saudi Arabia at 20:00 GMT. The attack caused a fire but no casualties, it said.

British maritime risk management group Vanguard also reported that the Saudi tanker Encelia had been hit.

The attack on the Layla has not been confirmed.

US Central Command (Centcom) said at 21:30 GMT it had launched strikes at Trump's direction "to further degrade Iran's ability to threaten civilian mariners and commercial vessels transiting regional waters".

The strikes targeted "Iranian military targets including maritime capabilities, missile and drone storage facilities, coastal surveillance sites, and air defense assets," it said.

Kuwait, Jordan and Bahrain soon reported responding to airborne threats, before Iran's military said they had targeted US assets in all three countries, according to AFP.

Iranian state media reported two people had been killed in US strikes on the country's south near its border with Iraq.

Meanwhile, the Iranian Revolutionary Guard (IRGC) said the Strait of Hormuz was "completely closed" after an explosion in the channel, Iranian state media reported.

The IRGC said it had stopped three oil tankers from passing through the strait.

One tanker caught fire and two others turned back after attempting to pass through a mined route south of the strait, according to Iranian state media.

It comes after Trump promised earlier on Wednesday to attack an Iranian bridge or power plant if its forces hit ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi later warned of an "eye for an eye" response to attacks on Iran.

On Tuesday, Trump told reporters he would "take care of the Houthis" should they obstruct the Red Sea as they had said.

Few details of the "maritime embargo" were given by the Houthis when it was announced on Monday, but a media official said they were closing the Bab al-Mandab Strait - the Red Sea's southern gateway - to Saudi vessels.

The Red Sea has become crucial for oil shipments from Saudi Arabia during the US-Israeli war with Iran, which has led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

Now, the threat from the Houthis risks further disruption to international shipping, with hostilities in the region having already led to global fuel prices fluctuating significantly.

So far, at least seven oil tankers have made U-turns close to Yemen since the embargo. Saree claimed the Houthis had "forced approximately ten ships to retreat and return".

The disruption in the Red Sea comes as peace negotiations have effectively stalled between the US and Iran.

Both countries signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) in June to halt military operations and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, as well as to reach an agreement to end the war over the following 60 days.

But three weeks after it was signed, Trump declared the ceasefire "over" after Iranian attacks on ships in Hormuz, and US strikes in response.

title: Wreckage of Pan Am plane that shaped aviation safety found 74 years on - Breaking News | Daily Mirror
summary:
BBC - The wreckage of a Pan American Airways plane has been found 74 years after it plunged into the Atlantic Ocean in a crash that prompted mandatory airline safety briefings.

The Clipper Endeavor was found 2,000ft (610m) below sea level off the coast of Puerto Rico with a sonar-equipped drone. It went down on 11 April 1952 following multiple-engine failure shortly after take-off.

Everyone onboard survived the impact - but passengers struggled to locate life vests and rafts as the plane rapidly sank. Of the 69 passengers and crew onboard, just 17 survived.

The disaster led to sweeping reforms in aviation safety, including compulsory pre-flight safety briefings on every commercial flight.

The expedition to find the wreckage was led by the Air/Sea Heritage Foundation in partnership with the Discovery Channel's Expedition Unknown show and several other organisations.

Last month, explorers discovered the ruins of the Douglas DC-4 aircraft using an autonomous sonar drone that detected the aircraft's fuselage and tail.

"We are all stunned and elated by this discovery, yet also humbled ⁠to remember what happened in that place so long ago," said Russ Matthews, president of the Air/Sea Heritage Foundation.

The plane had been carrying 64 passengers and five crew to New York when the pilot was forced to make a violent water landing.

The confusion that ensued became a "catalyst" for modern regulations mandating better flotation equipment on planes and preflight briefings on how to use it, aviation safety expert John Cox told AP.

Today, before every commercial flight, cabin crew are required to outline where a plane's exits are, as well as the location of life vests and how to inflate them.

"Every time you step onboard an airplane today, you are safer because of what happened to Clipper Endeavor and her passengers three-quarters of a century ago," said Expedition Unknown host Josh Gates.

Matthews, a maritime explorer and historian, first became interested in the crash in 2019, after reading about a luggage tag from the flight that had washed ashore in Florida.

He said in a statement that he had been "astonished that such an important story had largely faded from public memory".

He then began piecing together the aircraft's final moments using reports from the Civil Aeronautics Board, the predecessor to the US Federal Aviation Administration.

The breakthrough came after researchers uncovered records from a public hearing in Puerto Rico, including a map drawn by air force pilots who had witnessed the crash, which helped narrow down the search area.

Researchers used historical records and weather data from the time of the crash to identify the 10 square nautical miles of Atlantic Ocean seabed where the wreckage was likely resting.

An attempt to locate the wreckage in 2024 was abandoned due to poor weather - but Matthews said his team had been determined to return before the 75th anniversary of the crash.

A drone found the wreckage - which had broken into two sections - during its first pass of the search area on 2 June.

A follow-up photographic survey confirmed the wreckage was of the Clipper Endeavor, providing images that revealed the Pan Am logo and aircraft's name were still visible on the fuselage.

"To have a front-row seat to an expedition like this as it's unfolding is tremendous, and so I feel really lucky that we were able to be a part of it," said Gates, who was aboard the surface ship when the wreckage appeared on screen.

The discovery could offer fresh hope for the families of passengers of other planes that are presumed to have crashed in the ocean, such as Malaysia Airlines Flight 370.

It disappeared 12 years ago with 269 people onboard and, despite numerous searches in the Indian Ocean, has not yet been located.

The discovery of the Clipper Endeavor will be featured in a special episode of Expedition Unknown this Autumn.

title: Proposed Chartered Institute of media professionals to develop and maintain media standards - Breaking News | Daily Mirror
summary:
By Yohan Perera and Ajith Siriwardana

Colombo, July 23 (Daily Mirror) - The proposed Chartered Institute of Media Professionals is vested with powers to introduce, develop, maintain and monitor professional standards in the field of media, the Bill to this effect which was tabled in Parliament said.

Chartered Institute of Media Professionals of Sri Lanka Bill also provides provisions for the said institute to liaise and coordinate with local and foreign institutions having similar objectives to that of the institute.

The institute will be given powers to prepare a code of conduct in order to maintain professional discipline among its members.

The Chartered Institute of Media Professionals will function as a professional organization for professionals in the field of media. One of its main objectives is to enhance the standards, skills and practical training of its members, students of the institute and media professionals. It will also engage in accrediting media professionals after an evaluation,

It will conduct study courses for media personnel for which a fee will be charged.

The institute will also have the power to advise the media minister on any plan, programme or activity aimed at enhancing media professionalism in Sri Lanka.

The proposed institute will be governed by a council of elected members, but there will be an interim council which includes a secretary to the ministry of media, six other persons who will have proven knowledge, eminence and at least 20 years of experience in the media nominated by the secretary of the Media Ministry.

title: New Animal Welfare Bill: Rs. 250,000 fine, two-year jail for animal cruelty - Breaking News | Daily Mirror
summary:
Colombo, July 23 (Daily Mirror) - Those convicted of animal cruelty could face fines of up to Rs. 250,000, imprisonment for up to two years, or both, under Sri Lanka's long-awaited Animal Welfare Bill, which has now been published in the Government Gazette.

The proposed legislation, which is expected to be presented to Parliament, seeks to replace the century-old Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Ordinance (Chapter 475) with a tougher legal framework aimed at preventing cruelty and improving animal welfare across the country.

Under the Bill, it will be an offence to beat, kick, torture, overload, overbreed, abandon or poison animals, or intentionally deprive them of food, water or shelter. Keeping animals in cages or enclosures that do not provide sufficient space for movement will also be punishable.

The Bill imposes even harsher penalties for serious offences. Anyone found guilty of killing an animal in a cruel manner or intentionally killing or selling a pregnant animal could face fines of up to Rs. 500,000 and prison terms ranging from three to four years.

It also prohibits setting traps to injure or kill animals without reasonable cause, tying or restraining birds in a cruel manner, performing medical or surgical procedures on animals without proper qualifications, and using animals for cosmetic testing except in prescribed circumstances.

The proposed law further cracks down on organised animal abuse by banning sport hunting, shooting matches, animal fighting and baiting. Property owners who knowingly allow such activities on their premises could also face legal action.

The commercial sale of animals will also come under tighter regulation. Pet shops and breeding centres will be required to obtain licences from local authorities, while the sale of animals on streets or public places and the sale of pets to persons under the age of 16 will be prohibited.

The Bill introduces new welfare standards for transporting animals, requiring suitable vehicles, adequate space, proper loading facilities, and access to food, water and rest during long journeys. Violations could result in fines of up to Rs. 300,000.

To strengthen enforcement, all offences under the proposed law will be cognizable, allowing police to make arrests without a warrant. Designated Animal Welfare Officers will also be empowered to issue directions requiring owners to provide food, shelter or veterinary treatment, while courts will have the authority to confiscate animals and equipment used in cruelty offences upon conviction.

The legislation also provides for the establishment of an Animal Welfare Advisory Committee comprising representatives from government institutions, law enforcement, academia, animal welfare organisations and the livestock sector to oversee the implementation of the law.

If enacted by Parliament, the Animal Welfare Bill will mark Sri Lanka's most significant overhaul of animal protection laws, introducing stronger safeguards against cruelty and stricter penalties for offenders.

title: Dengue vaccine not the solution to current outbreak: Expert - Breaking News | Daily Mirror
summary:
Colombo, July 23 (Daily Mirror) - While saying that the dengue vaccine is not a solution to the current dengue epidemic, Consultant Physician Dr. Ananda Wijewickrama urged the public to seek immediate medical attention if they develop symptoms in order to reduce fatalities.

Speaking to Daily Mirror, Dr. Wijewickrama said the increasing number of mosquito breeding sites continues to drive the spread of the disease, making vector control the most important measure in curbing the outbreak.

He noted that several factors have contributed to the rise in dengue-related deaths, including patients delaying hospital treatment after the onset of symptoms and the strain placed on the healthcare system due to the large number of dengue patients requiring medical attention.

Dr. Wijewickrama urged the public not to ignore warning signs of dengue and to seek immediate hospital care, stressing that timely medical intervention significantly reduces the risk of severe complications and death.

Responding to a query on the dengue vaccine, Dr. Wijewickrama said the vaccine is not the answer to the current epidemic, as it cannot provide an immediate solution to the ongoing surge in cases.

He emphasised that eliminating mosquito breeding sites, preventing mosquito bites and seeking early treatment remain the most effective ways to control the outbreak and minimise fatalities.

Meanwhile, the number of dengue cases reported in Sri Lanka so far this year has increased to 78,125, according to the latest data released by the National Dengue Control Unit (NDCU).

The NDCU said 1,097 new dengue cases were reported yesterday (21), while 162 Medical Officer of Health (MOH) divisions across the country continue to be identified as high-risk areas for dengue transmission.

Furthermore, a total of 8,590 cases were reported in May, followed by 21,535 cases in June.

During the first 21 days of July alone, 22,749 dengue cases have already been recorded.

The NDCU also confirmed that 56 dengue-related deaths have been reported so far this year, with the case fatality rate standing at 0.07%.

title: Will the “tax shock” kill the Sri Lankan economy? - Breaking News | Daily Mirror
summary:
By Indika Hettiarachchi

Colombo, July 23 (Daily Mirror) - Under the latest IMF extended fund facility program, Sri Lanka has achieved substantial increase in tax revenue – to a level never seen in the history. Data show that for the first quarter of 2026, tax collections increased by an impressive 49 percent compared to same period last year. With GDP growing at 5.1 percent, and inflation below 2.5 percent, first quarter economic performance looks good on “IMF report card!”

But underneath this achievement, a major economic risk is building up steadily. This is because taxes are growing at an extremely faster rate than the economy itself. Such scenarios eventually lead to gradual economic decline. This is because increasingly larger chunk of economic value addition is absorbed by the state in the form of taxes.

Taxes growing faster than economy.

Economists measure the relationship between the economic performance (value addition), and taxes, with an indication called Tax Buoyancy Ratio (“TBR”). TBR is calculated as a ratio between the growth rate of taxes in response to growth rate in economic activity (or economic value addition).

Many countries use TBR in planning economic policies (but it is unlikely that Sri Lanka consider these aspects in planning tax reforms). Countries try to achieve a TBR marginally above one (1) enabling tax collection to grow in proportion to the expansion of economic activities. A TBR of one (1) implies that taxes grow in same proportion to the expansion of country’s economic activities. Higher TBR implies, a country’s tax revenues are growing at faster rate than the growth of real economic activities. High TBRs are not considered healthy as such situations can reduce economic output overtime

Data reveal that during the last three years Sri Lanka’s TBR skyrocketed to “extremely high” level compared to globally accepted rate closer to one (1). However, high TBR helped Sri Lanka to improve on the tax to GDP ratio which is a main target under any IMF support program.

As shown above, Sri Lanka’s TBR exceeded eight (8) in 2025. Historically Sri Lanka’s TBR has remained below one (1) throughout, reflecting Sri Lanka’s struggle to keep tax revenues in proportion to economic expansion.

Based on trends observed in the first quarter of 2026, and government plans to further increase tax collections, it is likely that the TBR will remain high during 2026 and beyond.

Countries like India target a long term TBR of around 1.2 to 1.5 to achieve a stable growth rate of around 6.5 to 7 percent while collecting enough taxes to support state spending plan. In fact India’s latest budget proposes to bring down TBR to 0.8 to stimulate economic growth.

Adjustment phase for the “tax shock”

Above discussed situation implies that at present Sri Lanka is going through a major adjustment phase for a “very high tax regime”. Adjusting from a TBR of below one (1) to a TBR in excess of eight (8) is more like facing “an economic shock” rather than going through an economic transformation as described by policy makers.

Moreover, recently issued Fiscal Strategy Statement by the President states that the estimated tax revenue growth for the year 2026 is only a 7 percent, whereas the actual tax collections up to date shows a growth close to 50 percent – which could be interpreted as an economic shock, rather than an fiscal achievement.

Impact of high tax buoyancy

It is difficult to find examples of countries that have gone through phases of extreme high TBRs such as Sri Lanka as such cases are exceedingly rare (and probably nonexistent). Hence forecasting the outcome of Sri Lanka’s current scenario is very difficult.

However, the medium term impact of high TBR is likely to be gradual decline in economic activities or value addition resulting in economic contraction. This will result in gradual business closures, rise in unemployment, etc. Already there are signs many SMEs are going out of businesses – especially in trades related to construction, retail, etc.

Perhaps the most dangerous impact of high TBR is the negative impact on low-income households. As Sri Lanka relies heavily on indirect taxes, even government (short term) efforts to stimulate economic activities will automatically reduce the living standards of low and middle income households. This is because any increase in economic activity results in disproportionate increase in taxes. This increase in taxes are transferred to low and middle income households disproportionately. When government relies heavily on indirect taxes, high TBRs impact poor consumers disproportionately. Gradually rising poverty level and associated developments such as surge in gold pawning are some indications of this reality. In fact, World Bank survey itself showed the indirect tax reforms in 2024 resulted in 2.2 percent increase in country’s poverty.

(The writer is an Investment, Project and Strategy Advisory professional. He has a Master’s degree in Economics from the University of Colombo, undergraduate degree in Business from the University of Wisconsin (USA), and is also a Chartered Financial Analyst (USA). Indika.h@jupitercapitalpartners.com)

title: El Nino to trigger unpredictable rainfall later this year, steps taken for food security - Breaking News | Daily Mirror
summary:
Colombo, July 23 (Daily Mirror) - With the development of El Niño conditions altering weather patterns in Sri Lanka, the government is planning for advancing the Maha cultivation season in a bid to avert any impact on food security, a Minister said yesterday.

Environment Minister Dr. Dammika Patabendi told Daily Mirror the Cabinet appointed committee met recently and discussed ways and means to brace for the situation.

According to the latest forecasts, he said that July, August and September would be dry months for Sri Lanka, but the north-east monsoon starting after would be heavier than normal.

“We want to advance the Maha season for rice cultivation this time to avert any impact on food security. Currently, there is no issue for drinking water supply and hydropower generation,” he said.

He said that a dry spell would prevail in January, February and March next year as a weather phenomenon due to El Nino.

El Niño conditions have developed in the tropical Pacific and are forecast to strengthen rapidly over the coming months, increasing the likelihood of heatwaves, droughts, heavy rainfall and other extreme weather events in many parts of the world, according to the World Meteorological Organization (WMO).

The 2026 El Niño is rapidly intensifying into a potentially record-breaking "super El Niño," bringing severe heat waves, erratic monsoons, and droughts to South Asia. Early south-west monsoon conditions are bringing localised heavy rains, but experts warn of a shift to drier conditions with reduced rainfall.
